(ii) Prove that the set $S$ of elements of $G$ not conjugate to any nonidentity element of $A$ has cardinality precisely $p^n$.

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$, and recall that $R$ is naturally a right $R$-module with respect to right multiplication. We denote this right regular $R$-module by $R_R$.

(i) Prove that $R$ is a division ring if and only if $R_R$ is a simple $R$-module.

(ii) Prove that $R$ is a division ring if and only if every nonzero right $R$-module contains a submodule isomorphic to $R_R$.
answer: (i) Submodules of $R_R$ are right ideals; if $R_R$ is simple each $x\ne0$ has a right inverse $y$, which itself has a right inverse $z$, and $x=z$. (ii) Over a division ring $r\mapsto vr$ is injective for $v\ne0$; conversely $R/M$ ($M$ a maximal right ideal) is simple and contains a copy of $R_R$, so $R_R$ is simple.

prompt:
Let $f(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, and let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be roots of $f(x)$ in the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$. Suppose $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq E\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ where $E$ is a (finite) Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

(i) Show that $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$.

(ii) Now assume that $E=\mathbb{Q}[\varepsilon]$ where $\varepsilon$ is a root of unity. Prove that $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$.
answer: (i) Extend $\alpha\mapsto\beta$ to an automorphism $\tau$ of a Galois field $F\supseteq E(\alpha,\beta)$; $\tau(E)=E$, so $\tau$ maps $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E$ onto $\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$. (ii) $\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ is abelian, so every subfield of $E$ is Galois and $\tau(\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E)=\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E$.

solutions.title: Extending the isomorphism $\alpha\mapsto\beta$
solutions.body:
Fact: if $E\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is finite Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\tau\colon F\to\mathbb{C}$ is a field embedding of some $F\supseteq E$, then $\tau(E)=E$ (normality).

**(i)** Let $F\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be the splitting field over $\mathbb{Q}$ of $g=f\cdot h$, where $E$ is the splitting field of $h\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$. Then $\alpha,\beta\in F$ and $E\subseteq F$. Since $f$ is irreducible, there is an isomorphism $\sigma\colon\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\to\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=\beta$. $F$ is a splitting field of $g$ over both $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]$ and $\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$, so $\sigma$ extends to an automorphism $\tau$ of $F$. Then $\tau(E)=E$ and $\tau(\mathbb{Q}[\alpha])=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]$, so $\tau(\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E)=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$ ($\tau$ is a bijection of $F$). Hence these fields are isomorphic via $\tau$.

**(ii)** If $E=\mathbb{Q}[\varepsilon]$ with $\varepsilon$ a primitive $m$th root of unity, then $\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ embeds in $(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$ and is abelian. So every subgroup is normal and every intermediate field of $E/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$. In particular $D=\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E$ is Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$, so $\tau(D)=D$ by the fact above. By (i), $\tau(D)=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$. Hence $\mathbb{Q}[\alpha]\cap E=\mathbb{Q}[\beta]\cap E$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field $F$, and let $S$ and $T$ be commuting linear operators on $V$. Assume that the characteristic polynomial of $S$ has distinct roots.

(i) Show that every eigenvector of $S$ is an eigenvector for $T$.

(ii) If $T$ is nilpotent, prove that $T=0$.
answer: (i) $T$ preserves each eigenspace of $S$, and these are $1$-dimensional. (ii) $T$ is diagonal in the eigenbasis of $S$, with nilpotent hence zero diagonal entries.

solutions.title: One-dimensional eigenspaces
solutions.body:
Let $n=\dim V$ and let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ be the $n$ distinct roots of the characteristic polynomial of $S$ (it splits since $F$ is algebraically closed). Each $\alpha_i$ is an eigenvalue with eigenvector $v_i$; eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent, so $v_1,\dots,v_n$ is a basis and each eigenspace $E_{\alpha_i}=Fv_i$ is $1$-dimensional.

**(i)** Let $v$ be an eigenvector of $S$, $Sv=\alpha_iv$, so $v\in E_{\alpha_i}=Fv_i$. Since $ST=TS$, $S(Tv)=T(Sv)=\alpha_iTv$, so $Tv\in E_{\alpha_i}=Fv$, i.e. $Tv=\beta v$ for some $\beta\in F$. Thus $v$ is an eigenvector of $T$.

**(ii)** By (i), $Tv_i=\beta_iv_i$. If $T^k=0$ then $\beta_i^kv_i=0$, so $\beta_i=0$. Hence $T$ kills the basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$, and $T=0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and let $V$ be a right $R$-module. Assume that $M_1,M_2,\ldots,M_n$ are finitely many $R$-submodules of $V$ with $M_1\cap M_2\cap\cdots\cap M_n=0$, and let $W$ be the (external) direct sum
$$W=V/M_1\oplus V/M_2\oplus\cdots\oplus V/M_n.$$

(i) Show that $V$ is isomorphic to an $R$-submodule of $W$.

(ii) Now suppose in addition that the modules $V/M_i$ are simple and pairwise nonisomorphic. Prove that $V$ is isomorphic to $W$. (Hint. First observe that $W$ has a composition series of length $n$.)
answer: (i) $v\mapsto(v+M_i)_i$ has kernel $\bigcap M_i=0$. (ii) $W$ has length $n$; $V$ embeds in $W$, so has finite length, and each $V/M_i$ is a composition factor of $V$, giving $n$ distinct factors; so $\ell(V)\ge n=\ell(W)$ and the embedding is onto.

solutions.title: Composition length
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $\theta\colon V\to W$, $\theta(v)=(v+M_1,\dots,v+M_n)$. It is an $R$-homomorphism with $\ker\theta=\bigcap_iM_i=0$, so $V\cong\theta(V)\subseteq W$.

**(ii)** Write $W_i=V/M_i$. The chain $0\subseteq W_1\subseteq W_1\oplus W_2\subseteq\cdots\subseteq W_1\oplus\cdots\oplus W_n=W$ has factors $\cong W_i$, which are simple, so it is a composition series and $W$ has length $n$. Hence $\theta(V)\cong V$ has finite length $\le n$, and so does $W/\theta(V)$, with $\ell(V)+\ell(W/\theta(V))=n$.

For each $i$, the chain $0\subseteq M_i\subseteq V$ refines to a composition series of $V$ whose top factor is the simple module $V/M_i$; by Jordan–Hölder, $V/M_i$ is a composition factor of $V$. The $V/M_i$ are pairwise nonisomorphic, so $V$ has at least $n$ composition factors (counted with multiplicity): $\ell(V)\ge n$. Therefore $\ell(W/\theta(V))=0$, i.e. $\theta(V)=W$, and $V\cong W$. ∎
